title: Everything we learned in 38 minutes at Harvard Business School
summary: Part 2 of the HBS series covers the soft skills: four leadership styles (servant, transformational, transactional, laissez-faire) illustrated with Starbucks, Apple, GE and Valve, and how to match style to company stage; then the three MBA networks (classmates, faculty, alums/investors) and tactical advice on maintaining relationships by giving first and treating contacts like friends.

ideas.idea: Leadership style directly shapes company culture, how performance is judged and how people grow, and performance translates to stock price.
ideas.detail: HBS treats leadership as its biggest pillar, teaching everything from command-and-control to servant leadership; the hosts outline four common styles.

ideas.idea: Servant leadership flips the hierarchy so the leader serves the people who work for them, and it pays off in the bottom line through more invested employees and better customer experience.
ideas.detail: Howard Schultz at Starbucks was among the first to give benefits to part-time baristas because employees cannot create a 'third space' for customers unless they feel it themselves, driving brand loyalty and revenue growth. The hosts note 'servant leadership' is a buzzy phrase worth dropping in conversation.

ideas.idea: Leading from the back and doing tasks alongside your team ('changing the printer cartridge') is more empowering than dictating from the front.
ideas.detail: Cherie co-created with her engineering and design teams at LinkedIn rather than telling them what to do; her boss Albert gave her two miniature terracotta soldiers on her promotion as a reminder that leadership is how we serve. Military-background classmates share the 'leaders eat last' mindset.

ideas.idea: Transformational leaders energize employees and create cult followings with a compelling vision, but the company needs a strong management team to survive their departure.
ideas.detail: Steve Jobs could look you in the eye and make impossible deadlines happen, and customers lined up overnight for iPhones to get whatever he dreamed up; Elon Musk is cited as a modern example. After Jobs, Tim Cook 'doesn't hit the same' even though Apple remains wildly successful.

ideas.idea: Transactional (carrot-and-stick) leadership uses clear rewards and penalties, epitomized by Jack Welch's 'rank and yank' at GE, where the bottom 10% were fired every year and the top 10% got outsized bonuses.
ideas.detail: GE massively outperformed in the 80s and 90s so this became the standard; Goldman let go the bottom 10% every year and Jean thought it was normal as a first job. Finance and consulting now call it 'up or out'.

ideas.idea: Up-or-out systems make people work harder and perform better, but at the expense of mental health and collegiality, and they fit sales orgs because results are judged within a quarter.
ideas.detail: Sales teams live by 'eat what you kill' with no allowance for extenuating circumstances, whereas product and engineering projects take multiple quarters or years, so discrete metrics are harder to apply. LinkedIn's top sales performers went to 'Club' trips, Zynga's top studio each quarter (60-120 people) went to Hawaii or Vegas, and early Snap salespeople kept 1% of the ad revenue they sold.

ideas.idea: Laissez-faire leadership has no official hierarchy and lets teams self-organize around self-identified goals, unleashing creativity that top-down strategy would never produce.
ideas.detail: Valve, the developer behind Steam, is the classic HBS case (also taught at Stanford). Jean notes Zynga's 'be your own CEO' motto and independent studios each with their own GM, CTO and head of product was laissez-faire applied at a company level.

ideas.idea: Laissez-faire only works with hungry, extreme-ownership personalities and small, high-trust teams; in big tech it breeds complacency and 'rest and vest'.
ideas.detail: Cherie's first reaction was 'nothing would get done' based on complacent big-tech teams where everyone looks around waiting; Jean counters that a two-person company like theirs is laissez-faire and could scale to six equally trusted people, though it is extremely fragile.

ideas.idea: Leadership styles are not one-size-fits-all; the best leaders weave elements of several styles into their own culture and approach.
ideas.detail: The value of learning the framework is being able to pull the elements that make sense for your personal style, industry and the culture you want to create.

ideas.idea: Match leadership style to company stage: laissez-faire for a two-person startup, transactional once you add people and need a rubric, then transformational once roles are clear and you aim for the stars.
ideas.detail: A transactional rubric lets people understand how they are measured; that base makes it possible to then ask people to go above and beyond their stated roles for something never done before.

ideas.idea: Networking is the biggest intangible benefit of an MBA, and it comes in three networks: classmates, faculty and professors, and alums and investors.
ideas.detail: Cherie used classmates as beta guests for her first podcast, Cherie's Corner, to work out the kinks; Stanford lecturers Joel Peterson and Glenn Kramon appeared on the podcast and Allison Kluger, a media and entertainment lecturer, advised on the sisters' post-graduation plan. Many alums are the investors.

ideas.idea: The power of a network is casual, reciprocal access: being able to text an expert friend without thinking twice and get a fast answer.
ideas.detail: When a company in an industry the sisters knew nothing about sent a collaboration contract, Jean texted a friend who is a foremost expert in that industry; she reviewed it and sent back a quick spreadsheet on how the math would work. This echoes Imran Khan's line that 'you're not really my friend unless I can just text you'.

ideas.idea: Maintaining relationships requires intentionality: when an article makes you think of someone, send it right away with a two-line note instead of waiting for networking to happen.
ideas.detail: Cherie regularly sends articles to Glenn Kramon, a former New York Times editor of 36-37 years, and uses the note to update him on what she and Jean are working on; do not spend 20 minutes rereading the email, just say 'thought of you, here is why' and send.

ideas.idea: Treat networking contacts like friends and text-message casually; people generally want to be friends with you and will treat you as a friend if you treat them as one.
ideas.detail: Jean admits she over-thinks and over-edits outreach emails, creating a barrier to sending; unless you are emailing the Prime Minister of Norway, a casual mindset is fine. Outreach is a muscle that gets less scary with repetition.

ideas.idea: To replicate an MBA network without the degree, offer help before asking for it; networking and mentorship are far more about giving than receiving.
ideas.detail: Networking gets a bad reputation because people take, take, take; before asking someone to mentor you, open your own network and resources first.

ideas.idea: Even a junior person can help someone five steps ahead: a relevant article is an overture anyone can make and it builds goodwill without trying.
ideas.detail: Cherie sent Glenn Kramon an article about LinkedIn profiles that matched his lecture topic; he replied within 15 minutes saying he would include it in his next lecture, a tangible difference from a small gesture.
